steps.title: Collapsing many rows into one number with aggregate functions
steps.lede: So far your queries returned one row per record. Aggregate functions let you compute a single summary across all of them.

blocks.text: Aggregate functions compute a single result from a set of input values — many rows in, one value out. `COUNT(*)` counts every input row; `COUNT(delivery_time_minutes)` counts only the rows where that column is not null, so it skips the two undelivered QuickCart orders.

The other four functions all ignore nulls. `SUM(delivery_time_minutes)` totals the non-null delivery times; `AVG` computes their arithmetic mean; `MIN` finds the shortest delivery; `MAX` finds the longest. One SELECT can compute all five at once, returning a single row of summary numbers.

before.caption: orders — one row per order, delivery_time_minutes shown (two NULLs)

result_of.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_orders, COUNT(delivery_time_minutes) AS delivered_orders, SUM(delivery_time_minutes) AS total_minutes, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_minutes, MIN(delivery_time_minutes) AS min_minutes, MAX(delivery_time_minutes) AS max_minutes FROM orders

after.caption: After COUNT(*), COUNT(col), SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX — one summary row, NULLs skipped by all except COUNT(*)

blocks.change_summary: Aggregate functions collapse all rows into a single summary row. COUNT(*) includes NULLs in the row count; the others skip them.

steps.title: COUNT(*) versus COUNT(column)
steps.lede: Make sure you know when the two forms of COUNT give different answers.

public.prompt: The `orders` table has 13 rows. Two of those rows have `delivery_time_minutes = NULL`. What does `COUNT(delivery_time_minutes)` return?

options.text: 11, because COUNT(column) counts only rows where that column is not null.
13, because COUNT counts every row regardless of nulls.
2, because COUNT(column) counts the null values.
NULL, because the column contains null values.

opt_a.message: Correct. COUNT(expression) counts only the rows where the expression is not null. Two nulls are skipped, leaving 11.

opt_b.message: Incorrect. COUNT(*) counts every row including nulls. COUNT(column) skips null values in that column.

opt_c.message: Incorrect. COUNT(column) counts non-null values, not null values. Use COUNT(*) - COUNT(column) if you want to count nulls.

opt_d.message: Incorrect. COUNT always returns an integer, never NULL. It counts the non-null values in the column.

correct.message: Exactly right. COUNT(delivery_time_minutes) skips the two NULL rows and returns 11.

incorrect.message: COUNT(column) counts only the rows where that column is not null. COUNT(*) counts every row. Here two rows have NULL delivery_time_minutes, so COUNT(delivery_time_minutes) = 11.

hints: Think about the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(a specific column).
Aggregate functions other than COUNT(*) skip NULL values in their input.

steps.title: Choosing the right aggregate for a question
steps.lede: Match the business question to the aggregate function that answers it.

public.prompt: A manager asks: 'What is the single longest delivery time recorded in the orders table?' Which aggregate function answers that question?

opt_a.message: Correct. MAX returns the largest non-null value in the column, which is the longest delivery time.

opt_b.message: Incorrect. SUM adds all values together, giving a total — not the single longest time.

opt_c.message: Incorrect. AVG computes the arithmetic mean across all non-null values, not the maximum.

opt_d.message: Incorrect. MIN returns the smallest value — the shortest delivery time, not the longest.

correct.message: MAX(delivery_time_minutes) returns the single largest value in that column — the longest delivery.

incorrect.message: To find the single largest value in a column, use MAX. SUM totals all values, AVG averages them, and MIN finds the smallest.

hints: The question asks for the single extreme value at the top end of the range.
Think about which function returns the largest value from a set.

steps.title: Compute the total and average order value
steps.lede: Write a query that returns a single row with the total and average of the amount column across all orders.

public.prompt: Write a query that returns a **single row** containing two values: the **total order value** (alias `total_amount`) and the **average order value** (alias `avg_amount`) across all orders in the `orders` table, in that column order (`total_amount` first).

files.content:
-- orders columns: order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes, order_date, region, amount, city
-- Return one row with two columns: total_amount and avg_amount.

blocked_syntax: ON with AND across several columns
subquery in FROM with an alias

solution_files.content:
SELECT SUM(amount) AS total_amount, AVG(amount) AS avg_amount
FROM orders;

tests.message_on_fail: Your query should return exactly one row with total_amount (SUM of amount) and avg_amount (AVG of amount). Check your column aliases and aggregate functions.

correct.message: Your query collapses all 13 rows into a single summary row using SUM and AVG — exactly what aggregate functions are designed to do.

incorrect.message: Use SUM(amount) AS total_amount and AVG(amount) AS avg_amount in your SELECT list, with no GROUP BY, so the aggregates run over all rows.

hints: Without GROUP BY, aggregate functions collapse the entire table into one row.
Use AS to give each aggregate a name: SUM(amount) AS total_amount.

steps.title: Splitting rows into groups with GROUP BY
steps.lede: A single AVG gives one number for all orders combined. GROUP BY lets you compute that average separately for each customer or region.

blocks.text: GROUP BY groups together rows that share the same values in the listed columns, combining each group into one output row. Any aggregate function in the SELECT list is then computed separately within each group. `SELECT customer_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id` returns one row per customer_id, each showing that customer's own average delivery time.

When a table is grouped, any column not listed in GROUP BY cannot appear in the SELECT list except inside an aggregate function. `SELECT customer_id, order_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id` would fail because order_id is neither grouped nor aggregated — each customer group contains several different order_ids, so SQL cannot pick one.

blocks.title: GROUP BY customer_id: rows split into per-customer buckets
blocks.alt_text: All orders rows are split into three buckets by customer_id. Each bucket collapses into one output row showing that customer's average delivery time.

steps.title: Diagnosing an ungrouped column error
steps.lede: Identify which column in a SELECT causes a GROUP BY error.

public.prompt:
A developer writes:
```sql
SELECT region, city, SUM(amount)
FROM orders
GROUP BY region;
```
What is wrong with this query?

options.text: `city` is not in the GROUP BY list, so it cannot appear in the SELECT list outside an aggregate function.
SUM(amount) cannot be used with GROUP BY; use a subquery instead.
The query is valid; SQL will pick any city value for each region group.
`region` must also be wrapped in an aggregate function when it appears in SELECT.

opt_a.message: Correct. `city` is not in GROUP BY and not inside an aggregate, so the database cannot determine which city value to show for each group.

opt_b.message: Incorrect. SUM works perfectly with GROUP BY — it computes the sum within each group. The problem is the ungrouped `city` column.

opt_c.message: Incorrect. Standard SQL (and most databases) reject this query. A column must be in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate to appear in SELECT.

opt_d.message: Incorrect. A column listed in GROUP BY can appear in SELECT without an aggregate — it is the grouping key. The problem is `city`, which is not in GROUP BY.

correct.message: Right. Every column in SELECT must either be in GROUP BY or wrapped in an aggregate. `city` is neither, so the query is invalid.

incorrect.message: When you use GROUP BY, every column in SELECT must either be listed in GROUP BY or appear inside an aggregate function. `city` is not grouped and not aggregated.

hints: Look at each column in the SELECT list and ask: is it in GROUP BY, or is it inside an aggregate?
The grouping key (region) is fine in SELECT. The problem is a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated.

steps.title: Count orders per region
steps.lede: Write a query that returns the number of orders for each region in the orders table.

public.prompt: Write a query that returns the **total order value per region**. The result should have two columns: **region** and **total_amount** (the sum of `amount` for that region). Order the result by **region ascending**.

files.content:
-- orders columns: order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes, order_date, region, amount, city
-- Return region and total_amount (SUM of amount per region).
-- Order by region ascending.

blocked_syntax: ON with AND across several columns
subquery in FROM with an alias

solution_files.content:
SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM orders
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY region ASC;

tests.message_on_fail: Your query should return one row per region with the total amount for that region, ordered by region ascending. Check your GROUP BY clause and column aliases.

correct.message: Your GROUP BY query correctly produces one row per region, each showing the sum of all order amounts in that region.

incorrect.message: Use GROUP BY region to form one group per region, then SUM(amount) AS total_amount to compute the total within each group. Add ORDER BY region ASC at the end.

hints: GROUP BY region tells SQL to form one output row for each distinct region value.
SUM(amount) computes the total within each group. Give it an alias with AS total_amount.

steps.title: Filtering aggregated groups with HAVING
steps.lede: WHERE filters raw rows before grouping. To filter on an aggregate result — keeping only customers whose average delivery time is high — you need HAVING.

blocks.text: HAVING filters out groups after GROUP BY has combined rows and computed aggregates. It acts on groups rather than raw rows, much like WHERE acts on rows. `SELECT customer_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING AVG(delivery_time_minutes) > 30` keeps only the customer groups whose average delivery time exceeds 30 minutes.

Expressions in HAVING can refer to grouped columns and to aggregate expressions computed over the group. You can use both in the same clause: `HAVING customer_id > 1 AND AVG(delivery_time_minutes) > 30` mixes a grouped column and an aggregate. WHERE and HAVING can also appear in the same query — WHERE removes raw rows before grouping, HAVING then filters the grouped result.

blocks.title: WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING: the filtering pipeline
blocks.alt_text: A pipeline: raw rows pass through WHERE (removes rows), then GROUP BY (forms groups), then HAVING (removes groups), producing the final result.

steps.title: HAVING: filtering groups after aggregation
steps.lede: Watch the error that appears when an aggregate is put in WHERE, and where HAVING sits relative to GROUP BY and ORDER BY.

segments.label: HAVING after GROUP BY: why WHERE cannot test an aggregate
segments.summary: Builds a query that counts rows per job title with GROUP BY, then tries to filter on that count with WHERE and gets an error saying an aggregate may not appear there. Switching to HAVING fixes it, and the speaker explains HAVING goes after GROUP BY because it works on the groups once they are aggregated. A second query keeps job titles whose average salary exceeds 45000, with HAVING placed after GROUP BY and before ORDER BY.

bridge.after: WHERE filters raw rows before grouping and HAVING filters groups after. The text above adds a query that uses both together.

steps.title: Writing HAVING on an aggregate expression
steps.lede: Check that you can place a HAVING clause correctly and reference an aggregate in it.

public.prompt: You want to keep only the regions whose total order value exceeds 10 000. Which clause and condition belong in the query after `GROUP BY region`?

opt_a.message: Correct. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. SUM(amount) is an aggregate expression, so it belongs in HAVING.

opt_b.message: Incorrect. WHERE runs before GROUP BY and cannot reference aggregate functions. Use HAVING to filter on aggregates.

opt_c.message: Incorrect. `amount` is a raw column value, not the group total. You need SUM(amount) to test the total for each group.

opt_d.message: Incorrect. WHERE cannot appear after GROUP BY, and it cannot reference aggregate functions. HAVING is the correct clause for filtering groups.

correct.message: HAVING SUM(amount) > 10000 filters the groups after aggregation, keeping only regions whose total exceeds the threshold.

incorrect.message: HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY has computed the aggregates. WHERE filters raw rows before grouping and cannot reference aggregate functions.

hints: Ask yourself: is the filter applied to individual rows (before grouping) or to groups (after grouping)?
For filtering, aggregate functions like SUM belong in HAVING, not in WHERE.

steps.title: Keep only regions with total amount above a threshold
steps.lede: Write a query that groups orders by region and returns only the regions whose total amount exceeds 10000 NGN.

public.prompt: Write a query that returns only the regions where the **total order value exceeds 20 000 NGN**. The result should have two columns: **region** and **total_amount** (the sum of `amount`). Order by **region ascending**.

files.content:
-- orders columns: order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes, order_date, region, amount, city
-- Return region and total_amount for regions whose total exceeds 20000.
-- Order by region ascending.

blocked_syntax: ON with AND across several columns
subquery in FROM with an alias

solution_files.content:
SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM orders
GROUP BY region
HAVING SUM(amount) > 20000
ORDER BY region ASC;

tests.message_on_fail: Your query should return only regions with total amount above 20000, ordered by region ascending. Check your HAVING clause and GROUP BY.

correct.message: Your query correctly groups by region, computes the total with SUM, and uses HAVING to keep only the groups above the threshold.

incorrect.message: Group by region, compute SUM(amount) AS total_amount, then add HAVING SUM(amount) > 20000 to filter the groups. WHERE cannot filter on aggregates.

hints: Start with the GROUP BY query from the previous exercise, then add a HAVING clause.
HAVING SUM(amount) > 20000 keeps only the groups whose total exceeds the threshold.

steps.title: Aggregating data with GROUP BY
steps.lede: Three tools that turn rows into summaries.

blocks.text: Aggregate functions — COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX — compute one value from many rows. The shape is always the same: many row values in, one summary value out.
GROUP BY answers 'per X' questions: list the grouping column, and each aggregate is computed once per bucket instead of once overall.
HAVING filters groups after aggregation, just as WHERE filters rows before grouping. Use WHERE to narrow raw rows, HAVING to narrow the grouped result.

remediation_steps.title: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) skips NULLs
remediation_steps.lede: The two forms of COUNT give different answers when a column has missing values.

blocks.text: COUNT(*) counts every input row regardless of nulls. COUNT(expression) counts only the rows where that expression is not null. The orders table has 13 rows but two have a NULL delivery_time_minutes — so COUNT(*) returns 13 while COUNT(delivery_time_minutes) returns 11.

result_of.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows, COUNT(delivery_time_minutes) AS delivered FROM orders

blocks.caption: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(delivery_time_minutes) — the difference equals the number of NULL delivery times

remediation_steps.title: SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX — which question each answers
remediation_steps.lede: Each function answers a different kind of question about a set of values.

blocks.text: SUM totals the non-null values — use it for 'what is the combined amount'. AVG computes the arithmetic mean — use it for 'what is the typical value'. MIN finds the smallest non-null value — use it for 'what is the fastest delivery'. MAX finds the largest — use it for 'what is the slowest delivery'. All four skip NULLs.

remediation_steps.title: Every SELECT column must be grouped or aggregated
remediation_steps.lede: When GROUP BY is present, SQL enforces a strict rule about which columns can appear in SELECT.

blocks.text: When a table is grouped, a column not listed in GROUP BY cannot appear in the SELECT list except inside an aggregate function. Each customer group contains several order_ids, so SQL cannot pick one to show — the query `SELECT customer_id, order_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id` fails. Fix it by removing order_id or wrapping it in an aggregate such as COUNT(order_id).

remediation_steps.title: HAVING expressions can reference grouped columns and aggregates
remediation_steps.lede: HAVING is more flexible than WHERE — it can test both the grouping column and any aggregate.

blocks.text: Expressions in HAVING can refer to grouped columns and to aggregate expressions computed over the group. For example, `HAVING customer_id > 1 AND AVG(delivery_time_minutes) > 30` tests a grouped column (customer_id) and an aggregate (AVG) in the same clause. WHERE cannot reference aggregates at all — that is why HAVING exists.
